do.text: The website asked for a parent's card number to 'pay for shipping'. The money was taken, and no gift card ever came.

ignore.text: You scrolled past. But the video keeps spreading, and your friend thinks it's real.

buddy.intro: Ooh, a new video popped up!
buddy.explain: It looks like a famous YouTuber is giving away free gift cards.
buddy.choices: You can tap the link, scroll past the video, or tell an adult. What would you do?

do.text: Uh oh! Let's see what went wrong.

ignore.text: Safe for now… but the fake video is still out there.

tell.text: Great call! A grown-up helped spot the fake!

stop.text: 'Only for the first 100 people' was trying to make you rush.

check.text: This video could be made with AI. Computers can copy a famous person's face and voice. Seeing it doesn't mean it's real.
Look at the name. This isn't the real channel. Scammers make names that look almost the same.
Famous people don't give free gift cards to strangers who tap a link. If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
This link goes to a strange website, not YouTube. Real prizes don't ask you to fill in a form there.
This is where the link goes. It wants you to pay for 'shipping' with a card. A real prize never costs money.
These happy comments are fake. Scammers write them so you'll trust the site.

recap.tell: Show a grown-up and say: 'I saw a video of someone famous giving away free gift cards. Is it real?'

tip.label: Free prizes are a trick
buddy: Anyone can make a video or a channel look real. Even check marks can be faked.
If a stranger online offers you a free prize, don't tap the link. Show a grown-up first.

summary.solution: If a stranger online offers you a free prize, don't tap the link. Show a grown-up first.
checks: Trusting a video just because it looks real
Channel names that aren't quite right
Prizes that ask you to pay
